textbook.filename: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Guide eBook.pdf
textbook.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Guide, Foundational (CLF-C02) Exam
textbook.accessiblePath: /workspace/attachments/f98e4c7f-d784-4bbe-be96-f67a3e84e81a/AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Guide eBook.pdf

reviewedPassages.use: Access patterns, resilience and class comparison structure. No proprietary questions copied.

differences: The 2023-created textbook predates guide version 1.3. The current guide supplies scope and weights.
The storage table includes historical dollar prices and RRS; it omits current Express One Zone. Do not treat that table as the current service catalog.
Textbook Deep Archive retrieval language must be qualified by retrieval option: current AWS docs distinguish Standard from Bulk, which may take up to 48 hours.
Book legacy support-plan and Snow-device examples do not override current vendor availability.

methodology.teaching: Read cited block content and distinguish explanation, reference instruction and service-name mention. No automated keyword/count classifier.
methodology.assessment: Task associations are inventories, not per-bullet proof. Reviewed batch questions have explicit option analysis; historical pools retain unresolved item-level audit work.
limitations: The separate current in-scope service page could not be retrieved through the web tool; domain pages and revision history were retrieved.
No exhaustive technical-document revalidation of every historical claim or every old distractor is claimed.
No observed learner transfer, psychometric calibration or exam-passing inference.

tasks.title: Define the benefits of the AWS Cloud
Identify design principles of the AWS Cloud
Understand the benefits of and strategies for migration to the AWS Cloud
Understand the AWS shared responsibility model
Understand AWS Cloud security, governance, and compliance concepts
Identify AWS access management capabilities
tasks.statusChangeReason: All ten official task bullets now have direct lesson evidence, including the previously missing root-only task, Parameters Store/Secrets Manager and policy ownership distinctions. The task has a large preexisting assessment pool plus focused original scenarios with option-level explanations; status is content coverage, not readiness.

tasks.title: Identify components and resources for security
Define methods of deploying and operating in the AWS Cloud
Identify AWS AI/ML and analytics services
Identify services from other in-scope AWS service categories
Understand resources for billing, budget, and cost management
Identify AWS technical resources and AWS Support options

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#benefits.heading: Benefits of the AWS Cloud
excerpts: Trade fixed up-front infrastructure purchases for variable usage-based spending where appropriate.
Provision resources quickly and experiment without waiting for a hardware procurement cycle.
Scale capacity to meet growth and use elasticity to react to changing demand.
Use global infrastructure to place workloads closer to users or meet resilience and sovereignty needs.
Use managed services to reduce undifferentiated operational work.
Do not answer 'AWS is always cheaper.' Cost depends on architecture, utilization, data transfer, commitments, and operations.

Operational efficiency is a business outcome, not a promise that AWS operates every customer decision. Managed services can reduce selected undifferentiated maintenance, while customers still own workload configuration, data, access, recovery and cost choices.

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#benefits-transfer.heading: Cloud benefit transfer decisions
excerpts: Unpredictable temporary demand spike | Elasticity | Agility or planned scalability
Planned larger workload | Scalability | Elasticity
Minutes instead of procurement weeks | Agility | Elasticity
New approved geographic market | Global reach | Automatic multi-Region redundancy
Continue through a component failure | Availability/resilience or fault tolerance | Durability
Provider purchasing power across customers | Economies of scale | Guaranteed savings

Cloud benefits enable choices rather than guaranteeing outcomes. Global infrastructure does not automatically create compliance or low latency; managed services reduce selected undifferentiated work but do not remove shared responsibility.

Read the requirement verb first: react to demand = elasticity; handle planned size = scalability; provision or experiment quickly = agility; geography = global reach; continue through failure = resilience/fault tolerance.

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#objective-clf-c02.heading: 1.1 — Cloud benefits under changing demand
excerpts: Agility shortens the experiment/provisioning cycle; elasticity adjusts allocated capacity as demand changes. Scalability describes the ability to handle different load sizes, including planned growth.

High availability reduces service interruption across independent failure domains. Fault-tolerant designs aim to continue operating through failures; both require architecture rather than merely buying a larger machine.

Managed services reduce undifferentiated work, but customers still design permissions, data protection, service configuration and recovery. Global infrastructure helps place workloads near users when data-governance requirements allow it.

Worked decision: A seasonal store has a stable baseline, brief unpredictable peaks and a requirement to stay available after an AZ failure. Which plan best combines elasticity and availability? Choose Use a load-balanced Auto Scaling tier across multiple AZs. Multi-AZ load balancing provides independent serving capacity; Auto Scaling responds to load. A larger single instance or a purchasing commitment does not remove its AZ dependency. Caching may help performance but does not make a single origin application available during failure.

Transfer exercise: Describe which requirement is met by Auto Scaling, which by multiple AZs, and which would still require database/session-state design. Then change the requirement to predictable growth and explain what changes.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain1.html

aws-clf-well-architected-decisions#six-p.heading: The six pillars
excerpts: Operate and improve processes | Operational Excellence
Protect systems and data | Security
Continue through component failure | Reliability
Use resources efficiently for the workload | Performance Efficiency
Avoid unnecessary spend | Cost Optimization
Reduce environmental impact | Sustainability

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#objective-clf-c02.heading: 1.2 — Distinguish the six Well-Architected pillars
excerpts: Operational excellence concerns operating, observing and improving workloads. Security concerns protecting information and systems; reliability concerns correct operation and recovery after disruption.

Performance efficiency selects and adapts resource types to requirements. Cost optimization avoids unnecessary spend for a required outcome. Sustainability considers resource/energy efficiency and environmental effects.

A decision can affect several pillars: rightsizing can improve cost and sustainability, while redundant capacity may increase cost while improving reliability. Identify the primary business requirement rather than assuming every question is cost optimization.

Worked decision: A team regularly rehearses recovery from failed components and verifies that the application resumes its required function. Which pillar is most directly addressed? Choose Reliability. Recovery and dependable operation are primarily reliability concerns. Faster resource choices are performance efficiency; environmental impact is sustainability; minimizing spend is cost optimization. Rehearsal and runbooks can also support operational excellence, but recovery is the stated outcome.
Transfer exercise: Classify a credential-rotation exercise, a deployment runbook, a cache experiment and a resource-cleanup policy by primary pillar; explain one cross-pillar tradeoff for each.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain1.html

aws-clf-well-architected-decisions#confu.heading: Pillar confusion pairs
excerpts: Reliability is continued operation and recovery; Performance Efficiency is selecting and using resources effectively.
Cost Optimization is avoiding unnecessary spend; Sustainability is reducing environmental impact.
Security protects identities, data and systems; Reliability addresses failure and recovery.
Operational Excellence concerns running and improving workloads; Reliability concerns resilience outcomes.

aws-clf-migration-decisions#strategy-cho.heading: Migration strategy chooser
excerpts: Move quickly with minimal code change | Rehost | Refactor before the deadline
Move while adopting selected managed-service improvements | Replatform | Call every change a refactor
Modernization and substantial redesign are acceptable | Refactor / re-architect | Assume rehost provides cloud-native benefits
Replace the existing application or product model | Repurchase | Migrate the old implementation by default
Workload is no longer needed | Retire | Spend effort moving it
Workload must remain where it is for now | Retain | Force a migration without a business constraint

aws-clf-migration-decisions#migration-re.heading: Migration resources and services
excerpts: Assess workloads, dependencies, or utilization | Application Discovery Service / Migration Evaluator | Assessment is not the migration strategy
Move servers or applications | AWS Application Migration Service | Supports migration; it does not prove compatibility
Move or replicate databases | AWS Database Migration Service | Replication does not prove schema or application compatibility
Transfer online data | AWS DataSync | Data transfer is not a full application migration
Hybrid storage scenario | AWS Storage Gateway | Hybrid storage is not the same as rehosting an application

aws-clf-migration-decisions#why-migrate.heading: Why organizations migrate
excerpts: Reduce data-center ownership | Move suitable workloads to managed/cloud infrastructure
Increase agility or revenue opportunity | Provision and experiment faster
Improve operational efficiency | Reduce undifferentiated infrastructure work
Reduce business risk or improve ESG performance | Choose an adoption plan that addresses resilience, governance, and resource efficiency

aws-clf-migration-decisions#database-rep.heading: Database replication
excerpts: Database replication can synchronize a source and target during a migration and help reduce downtime before cutover. It does not prove that schemas, data types, queries, transactions, or application behavior are compatible.
DMS is a migration/replication resource, not a migration strategy. Plan validation, cutover criteria, and rollback separately.

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#cloud-economics-t.heading: Cloud economics transfer decisions
excerpts: Oversized resource | Rightsizing | Autoscaling
Forgotten development resource | Stop/remove idle capacity | Availability
Server, facility and staffing comparison | Total Cost of Ownership | Monthly AWS bill
Capacity changes with demand | Elasticity/utilization | Guaranteed savings
Higher direct price but less maintenance | Managed-service tradeoff | Cheapest service
Physical host or portability restriction | Licensing/tenancy review | Automatic license portability

Cloud economics may shift portions of spending toward variable consumption and reduce idle capacity, but cloud is not automatically cheaper. Compare hardware, facilities, power, cooling, networking, staffing, licensing, resilience, transfer and operational labor.
Rightsizing chooses an appropriate resource size; autoscaling changes capacity over time. Cost optimization is a measured tradeoff, not simply selecting the lowest direct price.

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#objective-clf-c02.heading: 1.4 — Economics, licensing and total cost
excerpts: Compare total ownership: hardware refresh, facilities, power, cooling, staffing, resilience, software licenses and unused capacity. Usage-based cloud billing changes the cost model but does not guarantee savings.

BYOL eligibility depends on the vendor contract, product and tenancy. License-included services bundle eligible license cost into the service price. Dedicated Hosts may address physical-host licensing requirements but are not automatically cheapest.

Rightsize from measured CPU, memory, I/O and business demand before making long commitments. Consider data transfer, idle storage, resilience and operational effort; economies of scale do not remove these line items.

Worked decision: A server application is only busy during business hours. Its license has host-level restrictions. What should be evaluated before claiming AWS will be cheaper? Choose Utilization and shutdown options, license terms/tenancy, transfer, resilience and total operating cost. Total cost depends on demand, valid licensing and the chosen architecture. A large instance hourly rate, accounting classification or account count alone cannot establish savings.

Transfer exercise: Write an estimate with separate compute, storage, transfer, license and labor assumptions. Compare a continuously running design with an eligible scheduled design and identify which assumptions need measurement.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain1.html

aws-clf-cloud-concepts#economics.heading: Cloud economics
excerpts: Rightsizing avoids paying for unnecessary capacity.
Automation can reduce repetitive operational effort.
Economies of scale allow cloud providers to spread infrastructure costs across many customers.
Pricing models trade flexibility, commitment, interruption tolerance, and dedicated hardware for different costs.

aws-clf-security-compliance#responsibili.heading: Shared responsibility by service model
excerpts: Responsibility changes with the service. With EC2, the customer manages more of the guest operating system and workload configuration. With managed services such as RDS or Lambda, AWS manages more of the underlying platform, while the customer still owns data, identities, permissions, and application-level decisions.
Ask: what layer is AWS managing, and what remains under the customer's control?

aws-clf-security-compliance#objective-cl.heading: 2.1 — Service-dependent responsibility boundaries
excerpts: AWS operates physical facilities, hardware and foundational infrastructure. Customers choose access, data classification and application behavior. Shared controls such as patch management have different owners at different layers.

For EC2, customers patch guest operating systems and applications. For RDS, AWS operates more of the database platform, while customers control data, users, networking and supported configuration. For Lambda, distinguish AWS-managed runtime maintenance from the application code, libraries and configurations the customer supplies.
Managed services do not transfer responsibility for granting least privilege or deciding whether regulated data may be stored in a chosen location. Verify the actual service model in the scenario.

Worked decision: A company moves its database from EC2 to RDS. Which responsibility remains with the customer? Choose Choosing database-user permissions and protecting its data. The customer still controls database users, permissions and data requirements. Physical facilities and hardware remain AWS responsibilities. The move reduces some platform maintenance, not the need for data governance.

Transfer exercise: Create EC2/RDS/Lambda responsibility columns for physical security, guest OS, application dependencies, user access and customer data. Explain why one patching answer cannot be reused across all three services.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain2.html

aws-clf-security-compliance#objective-cl.heading: 2.2 — Governance, encryption and audit evidence
excerpts: Compliance evidence is contextual: Artifact supplies AWS reports/agreements, not an automatic certification of the customer workload. Verify the services, Regions, controls and regulatory requirements actually in use.

CloudTrail records supported account/API activity; event history is recent regional management activity, not a complete default object-access log. Configure trails/data events/retention for the investigation requirement. Config records supported resource configuration and rule evaluations; CloudWatch monitors metrics/logs/alarms.
At-rest encryption and TLS in transit protect different paths. KMS policies and IAM govern use of keys; encrypting a bucket does not by itself prevent an authorized principal from reading data.

Worked decision: An auditor needs AWS compliance reports, a record of who changed a security group and its historical configuration. Which combination fits? Choose Artifact, CloudTrail and AWS Config. Artifact supplies reports, CloudTrail identifies supported API changes and Config preserves configuration history when configured. Monitoring, threat/vulnerability detection and cost tools do not replace those three types of evidence.

Transfer exercise: Choose management versus data-event logging for security-group changes and S3 object reads, then define retention and centralized access. Explain what an AWS report does not prove about your own configuration.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain2.html

aws-clf-security-compliance#encryption.heading: Encryption and sensitive data
excerpts: Recognize encryption at rest versus encryption in transit. KMS manages encryption keys for integrated services; Secrets Manager stores and can rotate secrets. The exact service matters because 'key' and 'secret' are not interchangeable exam terms.

aws-clf-security-compliance#governance.heading: Governance, audit, and compliance
excerpts: AWS compliance reports and agreements | AWS Artifact
API/account activity | AWS CloudTrail
Configuration history and rules | AWS Config
Metrics/logs/alarms | Amazon CloudWatch
Threat detection | Amazon GuardDuty
Vulnerability management | Amazon Inspector
Web request filtering | AWS WAF
DDoS protection | AWS Shield

aws-clf-security-compliance#objective-cl.heading: 2.4 — Preventive controls, findings and security resources
excerpts: WAF filters supported application HTTP/S requests; Shield provides DDoS protection. Firewall Manager centrally manages supported security policies across accounts. GuardDuty detects threats; Inspector reports supported workload vulnerabilities; Macie discovers sensitive data in supported S3 content.

Security Hub aggregates findings/posture information. Trusted Advisor provides recommendations in supported categories, with access/features dependent on the current support offering. Findings do not automatically fix every issue; remediation still needs an owner and validation.

Use official security documentation, Knowledge Center, the Security Blog and security/compliance resources to verify behavior. Marketplace offers third-party products; neither a listing nor a security-service subscription guarantees compliance.

Worked decision: A security team needs centrally consistent web ACL policies across accounts and vulnerability findings for supported EC2 workloads. Which pair fits those separate needs? Choose Firewall Manager and Amazon Inspector. Firewall Manager manages supported policies across accounts; Inspector supplies vulnerability findings. GuardDuty detects threats rather than replacing vulnerability scanning, Artifact supplies reports, and Macie specializes in S3 data discovery.
Transfer exercise: Classify each service as primarily preventive, detective, governance or evidence retrieval. For a finding, specify who approves remediation and how you verify the risk is reduced.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain2.html

aws-clf-access-management#identity-choos.heading: Who or what needs access?
excerpts: EC2 application needs S3 | IAM role | Workload receives temporary credentials | Embedded access key
Employees use a corporate identity provider | IAM Identity Center / federation | Centralized workforce SSO | Shared IAM user
Organize IAM users | IAM group | Groups collect permissions for users | IAM role
A principal must be assumable | IAM role | Roles are assumable identities | IAM group
Store an application database password | Secrets Manager | Stores and can rotate application secrets | KMS key
Control encryption keys | AWS KMS | Manages encryption keys | Secrets Manager
Start with the actor: workforce, workload, or application secret. Then ask how it authenticates, where permissions come from, and whether credentials need to be long-lived.

aws-clf-access-management#root-mfa.heading: Root protection and MFA
excerpts: Protect the account root user with strong MFA and do not use it for routine administration.
Do not create or use root access keys for ordinary work; use named workforce identities instead.
Some account tasks may still require root. Check the current AWS root-user task guidance rather than memorizing an unverified list.

aws-clf-access-management#policies-least.heading: Policies and least privilege
excerpts: A permissions policy defines allowed or denied actions; a user, group, or role receives permissions but is not itself the permission rule.
Managed policies are reusable; inline policies attach directly to one identity.
Least privilege grants only the actions and resources required for the task.

aws-clf-access-management#users-groups-r.heading: Users, groups, roles, and federation
excerpts: An IAM user is a long-lived identity; an IAM group organizes IAM users and is not itself assumable.
An IAM role is an assumable identity that commonly provides temporary credentials to a workload, person, or cross-account principal.
IAM Identity Center and federation connect workforce identities to centralized AWS access without sharing IAM-user credentials.
Choose the identity pattern from the scenario rather than treating every access request as a new IAM user.

aws-clf-access-management#authentication.heading: Authentication versus authorization
excerpts: Authentication: who are you? | Password, MFA, federation, temporary session credentials
Authorization: what may you do? | IAM policies, role permissions, applicable resource policies, explicit denies

MFA strengthens authentication; it does not grant permissions. A password policy controls IAM-user password requirements; a permissions policy defines allowed actions. An explicit deny overrides an applicable allow at recognition level.

aws-clf-access-management#credentials.heading: Long-lived versus temporary credentials
excerpts: Access keys are programmatic credentials and should not be embedded in source code, AMIs, scripts, or repositories.
Prefer IAM roles and temporary credentials for workloads where supported.
Remove or rotate credentials that are no longer required and protect any remaining credentials as secrets.
IAM users can be appropriate when a specific long-lived identity is required; they are not categorically forbidden.

aws-clf-access-management#secrets-keys-r.heading: Secrets, encryption keys, and roles
excerpts: Application password or API secret | AWS Secrets Manager | KMS encryption key
Encryption key management | AWS KMS | IAM access key
Temporary workload permissions | IAM role | Stored application secret

aws-clf-technology-services#operate.heading: Ways to access and operate AWS
excerpts: AWS Management Console | Interactive browser-based administration
AWS CLI | Scriptable command-line access
AWS SDK | Programmatic access from application code
AWS CloudFormation | Repeatable declarative infrastructure as code

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.1 — Operate once, automate repeatedly
excerpts: The console is useful for interactive exploration. CLI commands support scripts; SDKs integrate AWS APIs into application code. CloudFormation models infrastructure declaratively as templates/stacks, including dependencies and repeatable changes.
A cloud deployment runs in cloud infrastructure; a hybrid design combines environments; on-premises remains a valid deployment context. Connectivity alone is not a migration strategy.

Choose repeatability and change control for repeated environments. IaC still needs permissions, parameter validation, reviews and safe handling of state/data; a template is not proof that every deployment succeeded.

Worked decision: A team must create the same reviewed network and application resources in several test environments. Which operating method best reduces manual configuration drift? Choose Versioned CloudFormation templates with reviewed parameters. CloudFormation describes repeatable infrastructure. Console memory is error-prone; additional keys do not encode infrastructure; CloudTrail records activity rather than provisioning the desired environment.

Transfer exercise: Compare a one-time diagnostic console task with a repeatable environment deployment. Describe the inputs, approval, change preview, verification and rollback for the repeatable workflow.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-clf-technology-services#domain3-tran.heading: Domain 3 transfer decisions
excerpts: Human, graphical, one-time inspection | Management Console
Repeatable shell administration | CLI and reviewed scripts
Application code calling AWS | SDK/API
Consistent versioned provisioning | Infrastructure as code / CloudFormation
One AZ failure | Multi-AZ within a Region
Regional disaster recovery | Multi-Region when permitted and justified
User proximity for supported edge delivery | Edge location
VM control | EC2
Event-driven function | Lambda
Kubernetes | EKS
Serverless containers | Fargate
Change capacity | Auto Scaling
Distribute requests | Load balancer

Exam traps: CLI is not an SDK; an API is not a command-line workflow; hybrid is not multi-cloud; a Region is not an AZ; an AZ is not an edge location; Multi-AZ is not automatically Multi-Region; ECS is not Kubernetes; Fargate is compute, not orchestration; Auto Scaling changes capacity while a load balancer distributes traffic.

Scope guard: CLF-C02 recognition does not require CLI command memorization, SDK programming, CloudFormation syntax, Kubernetes administration, EC2 model-number memorization, load-balancer configuration, or VPC implementation.

aws-foundation-cloud-global#global-infra.heading: Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations
excerpts: A Region is a geographic area that contains multiple isolated Availability Zones.
An Availability Zone is one or more data centers engineered to be isolated from failures in other AZs in the same Region.
Using multiple AZs is a common way to improve availability without leaving the Region.
Edge locations bring content or network services closer to users and are not the same thing as Availability Zones.
Multiple Regions can support disaster recovery, data-sovereignty requirements, and lower latency for globally distributed users.

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.2 — Availability scope and data residency
excerpts: A Region contains multiple isolated AZs; an AZ contains one or more data centers. A subnet belongs to one AZ; a VPC is regional. Edge locations support selected edge/network services and are not replacement AZs.

Multi-AZ design addresses an AZ failure within a Region. Multi-Region recovery addresses regional failure but adds replication, routing, permissions, cost and operational work. It must be compatible with residency restrictions.

For residency, select permitted processing/storage locations; do not assume more Regions are always required or allowed. For global content delivery, distinguish edge caching from deploying a second application/database Region.

Worked decision: Customer records must stay in one permitted Region, but the application must survive an AZ failure. Which design best fits? Choose Deploy the required tiers across AZs in that permitted Region. Multiple AZs can improve availability while retaining the selected Region. Arbitrary cross-Region copies can violate the stated residency constraint, an edge location is not a database failure domain, and one subnet cannot span AZs.
Transfer exercise: Draw Region, VPC, AZ and subnet boundaries. Change the requirement to regional DR and list which governance, replication and recovery decisions now require approval.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-foundation-compute-storage#compute.heading: Compute choices
excerpts: Amazon EC2 | You need virtual machines and control over the operating system.
AWS Lambda | Run event-driven code without managing servers.
Amazon ECS | Run containers with AWS container orchestration.
Amazon EKS | Run Kubernetes workloads with a managed Kubernetes control plane.
AWS Fargate | Run supported containers without managing the underlying servers.
Auto Scaling changes capacity; Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic. They often work together, but they solve different problems.

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.3 — Compute families and scaling roles
excerpts: General-purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized and storage-optimized instance families fit different bottlenecks. Measure CPU, memory, local I/O and networking rather than defaulting to the largest instance.

EC2 provides guest-OS control. Lambda runs suitable function workloads without server management. ECS and EKS orchestrate containers; Fargate supplies serverless compute for supported ECS/EKS workloads. These are different layers, not interchangeable product names.
Auto Scaling maintains/adjusts capacity; a load balancer distributes requests. Deployment across AZs and externalized session state are separate availability decisions.

Worked decision: A database cache has high memory pressure but low CPU utilization. It must continue running on EC2. Which first change should be evaluated? Choose A memory-optimized instance family sized from measurements. The stated bottleneck is memory. Compute or local-storage optimization alone does not address it. Purchase model and interruption tolerance are separate from resource-family suitability.
Transfer exercise: Match a batch CPU job, memory cache, disposable local scratch job and event-triggered function to a resource model. Explain when scaling and load balancing are both necessary.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.4 — Database models and migration responsibilities
excerpts: RDS/Aurora fit relational workloads; DynamoDB provides key-value/document access patterns; ElastiCache supplies in-memory caching; Redshift is a data warehouse. These are workload models, not a ranking of universally better databases.

An EC2-hosted database gives more OS/database administration control and more responsibility. Managed databases reduce selected maintenance tasks but still require access, backup, recovery, network and engine choices.

DMS supports supported database migration/replication with cutover planning. Heterogeneous migrations can require schema conversion and application changes; moving rows does not prove all procedures, types and queries are compatible.

Worked decision: A business moves an application to a different managed relational engine. It needs existing data and compatible schema/application behavior. What should be planned? Choose Assess schema/application compatibility and use supported migration/replication tools with validation. Schema conversion, application compatibility and validation remain necessary during heterogeneous migration. DMS data movement is not a guarantee that all engine features migrate unchanged. A cache and DNS data do not replace the relational workload.

Transfer exercise: Compare managed relational, EC2-hosted relational, NoSQL and warehouse requirements. Plan a migration test with row counts, integrity checks, application queries and a rollback window.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-foundation-network-database#database.heading: Database positioning
excerpts: Amazon RDS / Aurora | Managed relational database workloads
Amazon DynamoDB | Managed key-value/document NoSQL workloads at scale
Amazon ElastiCache | In-memory caching
Amazon Redshift | Managed data warehousing and analytics

For a single-standby RDS Multi-AZ DB instance, the standby is for availability, not reads. Multi-AZ DB clusters have readable standbys. Asynchronous read replicas offload reads and can lag; Aurora has its own reader/failover architecture.

aws-clf-technology-services#data-network.heading: 3.4–3.6 — Data, network and storage decisions
excerpts: Relational SQL | RDS / Aurora
Key-value or document access | DynamoDB
Repeated reads and low latency | ElastiCache
Move or replicate database data | DMS
Convert schema or database code | SCT
Logically isolated network | VPC
Stateful resource traffic | Security group
Stateless subnet traffic | Network ACL
DNS | Route 53
Encrypted internet connection | VPN
Dedicated private path | Direct Connect
Object storage | S3
Persistent EC2 block | EBS
Temporary local block | Instance store
Shared file storage | EFS / FSx
Hybrid storage integration | Storage Gateway
Centralized backup policy | AWS Backup

Exam traps: RDS is not DynamoDB; DynamoDB is not a cache; DMS moves data while SCT helps convert schema/code; VPC is not a subnet; security groups are stateful/resource-level while NACLs are stateless/subnet-level; VPN is not Direct Connect; Direct Connect is not an encryption guarantee; S3 is not EBS; EBS is not instance store; lifecycle is not backup.

Selection guard: name the data or traffic model first, then compare availability, access pattern, operations, recovery, residency and cost. Do not choose a service from a single keyword such as ‘database’, ‘network’ or ‘archive’. Scope guard: CLF-C02 recognition does not require SQL syntax, database-engine administration, DynamoDB key design, cache-cluster configuration, route-table or CIDR implementation, security-rule authoring, Direct Connect provisioning, lifecycle JSON, EBS tuning or file-system mount commands.

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.5 — Network services and traffic paths
excerpts: VPC routes select next hops; security groups and NACLs filter traffic at different scopes. Stateful security groups track return traffic; stateless NACL rules require the appropriate return path.

Direct Connect is dedicated private connectivity, not default end-to-end encryption. Site-to-Site VPN supplies IPsec tunneling. PrivateLink exposes supported services privately; Transit Gateway provides hub routing; peering directly connects compatible VPCs without transitive routing.

Route 53 supplies DNS and routing policies. CloudFront supplies content delivery/caching; Global Accelerator improves paths to supported regional TCP/UDP endpoints. Match content distribution versus network acceleration requirements.

Worked decision: A company wants a private dedicated link to AWS and also requires encryption in transit. Which statement is correct? Choose Evaluate Direct Connect plus a supported encryption design such as VPN or eligible MACsec, as required. Dedicated/private transport and encryption are different properties. Direct Connect does not encrypt by default; an appropriate VPN/MACsec/application design must meet the actual scope. DNS and NAT do not supply the required physical circuit.
Transfer exercise: Trace a DNS lookup, content download and private EC2 outbound request. Identify routing, addressing, filtering and encryption separately for each path.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-foundation-network-database#vpc.heading: VPC building blocks
excerpts: A VPC is a logically isolated network in AWS.
Subnets divide VPC address space and are associated with a single Availability Zone.
Route tables determine where traffic is sent.
An internet gateway enables internet routing for appropriately configured public resources.

In the zonal public-NAT IPv4 design, private-subnet default routes point to a public NAT gateway with an EIP and a path through the VPC internet gateway. A private NAT cannot provide internet egress through an IGW. Native IPv6 outbound-only egress uses an egress-only IGW; NAT64/DNS64 serves different translation requirements. Regional NAT is a separate current multi-AZ option.

aws-foundation-network-database#network-.heading: Security groups and network ACLs
excerpts: Security group | Stateful control associated with supported resources such as network interfaces.
Network ACL | Stateless subnet-level control with ordered allow/deny rules.
For SAA scenarios, ask where the control applies and whether return traffic is automatically allowed.

aws-foundation-network-database#dns-edge.heading: DNS, edge, and hybrid connectivity
excerpts: Amazon Route 53 | DNS, domain registration, health checks, and routing policies
Amazon CloudFront | Content delivery through edge locations
AWS Direct Connect | Dedicated private network connectivity to AWS
AWS Site-to-Site VPN | Encrypted VPN connectivity over the internet
AWS Transit Gateway | Hub for connecting multiple VPCs and on-premises networks

aws-clf-technology-services#objective-cl.heading: 3.6 — Storage classes, retrieval and recovery
excerpts: S3 is object storage, EBS is persistent block storage in an AZ, instance store is ephemeral, and EFS/FSx provide file-system options. Select access model, sharing, persistence, latency and availability before price.

S3 Standard suits frequent access; Standard-IA and One Zone-IA introduce access/minimum-duration and resilience considerations. Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive have different access/retrieval characteristics. Intelligent-Tiering monitors eligible access patterns; optional archive tiers change retrieval behavior.

Lifecycle can transition or expire eligible objects by date/age; versioning, replication and AWS Backup serve different recovery needs. A transition policy is not an immutable-retention control, and a replica is not proof of a tested restore.

Worked decision: An archive can tolerate long retrieval times and is rarely accessed, but must remain recoverable for years. What must be checked before choosing the cheapest S3 archival class? Choose Retrieval time/cost, minimum-duration charges, resilience and retention requirements. Storage price alone omits retrieval delay and charges, retention and resilience requirements. Bucket naming and unrelated EC2 sizing do not remove archival retrieval behavior.

Transfer exercise: Compare classes for hot assets, infrequently read documents and a long-term archive. State whether each needs immediate retrieval, AZ resilience, version recovery or enforced retention.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain3.html

aws-foundation-compute-storage#s3.heading: S3 durability, classes, lifecycle, and access
excerpts: S3 stores objects in buckets and is designed for very high durability.
Storage classes trade retrieval characteristics and access assumptions for cost.
Lifecycle rules automate transitions or expiration based on policy.
Versioning helps protect against accidental overwrite or deletion scenarios.
Presigned URLs provide time-limited access without making an object public.

aws-foundation-compute-storage#storage-m.heading: Object, block, and file storage
excerpts: Object storage at massive scale | Amazon S3
Block volume for an EC2 instance | Amazon EBS
Ephemeral block storage tied to host lifecycle | EC2 instance store
Shared Linux-style file system | Amazon EFS
Managed specialized file systems | Amazon FSx

aws-clf-technology-services#hybrid.heading: Hybrid and transfer services
excerpts: AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity.
Site-to-Site VPN uses encrypted tunnels over the internet.
Storage Gateway connects on-premises environments with AWS storage.

Snow devices are a historical offline/edge recognition cue: Snowball Edge is restricted to existing customers and Snowcone is discontinued. Do not recommend ordering Snow devices for an unspecified new customer.

aws-foundation-compute-storage#transfer-.heading: Transfer and backup patterns
excerpts: DataSync provides managed online transfers; Storage Gateway supplies hybrid file/volume/tape interfaces. AWS Backup centralizes supported backup policies. Snowball Edge is restricted to existing customers since November 7, 2025, and Snowcone is discontinued. For new physical-transfer designs evaluate Data Transfer Terminal or partners; Outposts addresses relevant edge-compute needs.

aws-clf-ai-analytics#ai-decision-table.heading: AI requirement → service
excerpts: Extract sentiment, entities, or key phrases from text | Amazon Comprehend | Prebuilt natural-language analysis | Amazon Translate changes language; it does not provide sentiment analysis
Build a chatbot or conversational voice/text interface | Amazon Lex | Conversational interface with intents | Amazon Q is an AI assistant; SageMaker AI is for building/training models
Convert text into spoken audio | Amazon Polly | Text-to-speech | Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text
Convert a recording into a searchable transcript | Amazon Transcribe | Speech-to-text | Amazon Polly produces audio from text
Translate text between supported languages | Amazon Translate | Machine translation | Amazon Comprehend analyzes language rather than translating it
Recognize objects or activity in images or video | Amazon Rekognition | Image and video analysis | Amazon Textract extracts text and fields from documents
Extract printed text and form fields from scanned documents | Amazon Textract | Document and form analysis | Amazon Rekognition analyzes visual content
Build, train, and deploy a custom ML model | Amazon SageMaker AI | Managed model-development workflow | A task-specific AI service is simpler when it already fits the requirement
Use an AWS AI assistant for work or information tasks | Amazon Q | AWS AI assistant capability | Lex is for building a conversational interface into an application

aws-clf-ai-analytics#analytics-decision-.heading: Analytics requirement → service
excerpts: Run ad hoc SQL directly over data in S3 | Amazon Athena | Serverless query service; not a permanent warehouse
Process large datasets with managed big-data frameworks | Amazon EMR | Managed cluster processing; no Hadoop administration required here
Integrate, prepare, transform, or catalog data | AWS Glue | ETL and data catalog concepts
Ingest and process live streaming data | Amazon Kinesis | Streaming telemetry or events; not a durable work queue
Search and analyze indexed logs or documents | Amazon OpenSearch Service | Search/log analytics over indexed data
Create executive BI dashboards | Amazon Quick / Amazon Quick Sight capability | Current naming is Amazon Quick; Quick Sight is the BI capability
Run analytics against a managed data warehouse | Amazon Redshift | Warehouse workload; not an OLTP database
Start with the verb: query, transform, stream, search, visualize, or warehouse. Then choose the service whose primary job matches that verb.

aws-clf-other-service-categories#applica.heading: Application integration
excerpts: Durable asynchronous queue between producers and consumers | Amazon SQS | queue | SNS fanout
Publish one message to many subscribers | Amazon SNS | publish/fanout | SQS queue
Route events to targets using rules | Amazon EventBridge | event routing | Step Functions
Coordinate multiple workflow steps | AWS Step Functions | workflow orchestration | EventBridge

aws-clf-other-service-categories#busines.heading: Business applications
excerpts: Cloud contact center | Amazon Connect | Amazon SES
Send application or transactional email | Amazon SES | Amazon SNS

aws-clf-other-service-categories#custome.heading: Customer enablement
excerpts: A requirement for AWS business or technical assistance points to AWS Support. Objective 3.8 recognition is intentionally brief; use the Domain 4 support material for plan and entitlement detail.

aws-clf-other-service-categories#develop.heading: Developer tools
excerpts: Compile, build, or test source code | AWS CodeBuild | build | CodePipeline
Orchestrate software delivery stages | AWS CodePipeline | pipeline | CodeBuild
Trace a request across distributed services | AWS X-Ray | distributed tracing | CloudWatch

aws-clf-other-service-categories#end-use.heading: End-user computing
excerpts: Stream an application to a user | Amazon AppStream 2.0 | application | WorkSpaces
Provide a managed virtual desktop | Amazon WorkSpaces | desktop | AppStream 2.0
Provide secure browser-only access to websites/apps | Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser | browser | WorkSpaces

aws-clf-other-service-categories#fronten.heading: Frontend and mobile
excerpts: AWS Amplify is the recognition-level choice for developing and deploying frontend web or mobile applications. The cue is the frontend/mobile application requirement, not a request to build or orchestrate backend source-code delivery.

aws-clf-other-service-categories#interne.heading: Internet of Things
excerpts: AWS IoT Core connects and manages interactions with IoT devices and supports device-to-cloud messaging at recognition level. Do not expand this review into IoT Device Defender or Greengrass; they are not required answers in this focused service set.

aws-clf-billing-support#pricing.heading: Pricing model decisions
excerpts: Maximum flexibility, no long commitment | On-Demand
Steady usage with commitment | Savings Plans or eligible Reserved pricing
Interruptible fault-tolerant workloads | Spot
Physical host visibility/licensing requirements | Dedicated Host
Reserve capacity in an Availability Zone | Capacity Reservation
Dedicated physical host with host-level visibility or licensing needs | Dedicated Host
Dedicated hardware tenancy without host allocation control | Dedicated Instance

aws-clf-billing-support#pricing-factors.heading: Storage and data-transfer pricing factors
excerpts: Storage cost depends on class or tier, stored volume, requests, retrieval charges, minimum storage duration where applicable, lifecycle transitions, and data transfer—not only GB stored.
Rarely accessed data with long retrieval tolerance should lead you to compare archival-class behavior and retrieval costs rather than automatically choosing the lowest storage rate.
Inbound and outbound transfer may price differently. Inter-Region, inter-AZ, and service-to-service transfer have service-specific rules, so architecture placement affects cost.

Free Tier benefits have service, usage, account, and time eligibility conditions. Check the current Free Tier terms and monitor usage; never treat a Free Tier label as an unlimited or permanent waiver.
Pricing questions are relative decisions: identify commitment, interruption tolerance, capacity guarantee, tenancy, storage access pattern, and transfer path before comparing rates.

aws-clf-billing-support#objective-clf-c0.heading: 4.1 — Purchase commitments, capacity and transfer
excerpts: On-Demand is flexible pay-as-you-go compute without a long-term commitment. Savings Plans provide pricing savings in exchange for an eligible compute-usage commitment; Reserved Instance pricing is more closely tied to instance configuration and scope/attribute rules. A regional RI does not reserve capacity; a zonal RI does reserve matching capacity in its selected AZ. Savings Plans provide discounts without capacity reservation. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation is a separate capacity option.

Spot fits interruption-tolerant work and spare capacity; Dedicated Hosts address eligible physical-host/tenancy needs. Compare total cost and restart overhead instead of assuming any model always wins.

Review RI flexibility and eligible consolidated-billing discount sharing within Organizations. Data transfer into/out of services, across AZs/Regions and to users has service-specific rules. Storage pricing includes requests, retrieval, minimum durations and transitions as well as stored GB.

Worked decision: A team buys a regional RI discount and then assumes a particular AZ is guaranteed to have capacity at launch time. What is the problem? Choose A regional discount and an AZ capacity reservation are different commitments. Discount eligibility does not guarantee zonal capacity. Review the particular RI scope and a suitable capacity-reservation design when launch availability matters. Savings Plans do not reserve unlimited capacity, and Spot remains interruptible.

Transfer exercise: Compare a commitment discount, a capacity reservation and dedicated tenancy for the same workload. Add transfer and archive-retrieval costs to show why hourly compute price is not the whole estimate.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain4.html

Transfer example: Uploading data into AWS is generally not charged for inbound transfer, while sending data out to the internet or between Regions may incur transfer charges; the exact path and service matter. AWS states that most inbound and same-Region service-to-service transfer is not charged, but exceptions apply. For example, same-Region S3 downloads within AWS can avoid data-transfer charges, while GET request charges still apply. Compare the current pricing rules for each service and direction; do not treat “inbound is free” or “same Region is free” as universal.

aws-clf-billing-support#objective-clf-c0.heading: 4.2 — Estimate, observe, allocate and alert
excerpts: Pricing Calculator estimates a planned design from assumptions. Cost Explorer analyzes costs/usage and supports forecasts; detailed billing exports support more granular analysis. None of these validates a bad architecture assumption automatically.

Budgets can alert on actual/forecast amounts and utilization/coverage; notifications and billing data have delay. A budget is not an instantaneous spending cap. Any budget action requires separate supported configuration and permissions.

Organizations provides consolidated billing. Apply and activate eligible cost-allocation tag keys for billing analysis; merely attaching a tag does not guarantee its immediate appearance in reports. Account boundaries and allocation rules determine financial ownership.
The Cost and Usage Report provides detailed cost and usage records for granular analysis. It is a reporting dataset, not a real-time spending cap.

Worked decision: Resources are tagged Project=Website, but finance cannot group their costs by that key. What should be checked first? Choose Whether the user-defined tag key is activated for cost allocation and billing data has become available. User-defined cost allocation tags need activation and time to appear in billing data. Network rules, CloudTrail and larger instances do not activate billing dimensions.

Transfer exercise: Build a paper estimate, define actual/forecast budget alerts and describe the notification test. Activate a cost tag in a permitted training account or explain the workflow without creating paid resources.
Scope reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/cloud-practitioner-02/cloud-practitioner-02-domain4.html
Determine the amount owed for a closed billing period | Issued invoice / Bills page; the invoice is the final amount owed.
See the current month before close | Bills page shows an estimate based on metered usage to date.
Analyze trends, forecasts, or finer dimensions | Cost Explorer; its analytical presentation can differ from invoice/billing data.
Inspect detailed usage and cost records | Cost and Usage Report; use it for granular analysis, not as the payable invoice.

If Cost Explorer and an invoice differ, use the invoice to identify the amount owed for a closed period. The datasets can differ in timing, grouping, granularity, rounding, and presentation of discounts, credits, refunds, or taxes. Use Cost Explorer to analyze patterns and investigate the difference.

aws-clf-billing-support#cost-tools.heading: Cost tools
excerpts: Estimate a planned architecture | AWS Pricing Calculator
Analyze historical/current spend | AWS Cost Explorer
Set a threshold and alert | AWS Budgets
Detailed billing and usage data | AWS Cost and Usage Report
Allocate spend by project/team | Cost allocation tags

aws-clf-billing-support#organizations.heading: Organizations and consolidated billing
excerpts: AWS Organizations can centralize account management and consolidated billing. Cost allocation and account structure help separate ownership while centralizing financial visibility.

aws-clf-billing-support#support.heading: Technical resources and support
excerpts: Use official AWS documentation, whitepapers, Prescriptive Guidance, Knowledge Center, re:Post, and support resources based on the need.
Support-plan questions test which level of guidance and response is appropriate; avoid memorizing old plan details without checking the current AWS Support page.
AWS Partner Network includes partners that provide software and professional services around AWS.

aws-clf-billing-support#support-plan-cur.heading: Current support-plan cues
excerpts: Account, billing, documentation, community and general resources | Basic Support
Production workloads needing 24/7 technical support and AWS expert engagement | Business Support+
Business-critical workloads needing strategic guidance and a Technical Account Manager | Enterprise Support
Mission-critical workloads needing the highest proactive operations/resilience assistance | Unified Operations

Developer Support and Business Support stopped accepting new subscriptions on December 2, 2025 and are scheduled for discontinuation on January 1, 2027. Enterprise On-Ramp is also transitional. Do not present these legacy names as the current standard paid-plan lineup. Verify entitlements and response details on the current AWS Support plan page.

aws-clf-billing-support#objective-clf-c0.heading: 4.3 — Support choices and escalation resources
excerpts: Current AWS documentation lists Basic Support and enhanced offerings including Business Support+, Enterprise Support and Unified Operations. Basic is the general account/billing/documentation baseline; Business Support+ cues production technical support, Enterprise cues strategic guidance/TAM support, and Unified Operations cues the highest proactive operations and resilience assistance. Compare current entitlements rather than memorizing retired plan names or treating response targets as resolution guarantees.

Use documentation, re:Post/Knowledge Center and Prescriptive Guidance for self-service knowledge. Support Center handles support cases; support entitlements determine the available channel and technical response. Trusted Advisor and AWS Health/Health API expose different recommendation and health signals.

AWS Partners include software vendors and integrators; Marketplace distributes third-party products and purchasing entitlements. Professional Services and solutions architects address different assistance needs. Report suspected AWS-resource abuse through the appropriate Trust and Safety process, rather than sending it to an unrelated billing alert.

Developer Support and Business Support stopped accepting new subscriptions on December 2, 2025 and are scheduled for discontinuation on January 1, 2027; Enterprise On-Ramp is also transitional. The current study set recognizes Basic Support, Business Support+, Enterprise Support, and Unified Operations as the current plan names.

Worked decision: A team needs information about an AWS event affecting its account resources, rather than a general architecture recommendation. Which resource should it check? Choose AWS Health and the relevant Health API/dashboard information. AWS Health provides relevant health/event information; Trusted Advisor recommendations and cost estimation serve different purposes. Marketplace and infrastructure templates do not replace the event/health signal.
Authoritative service reference | AWS documentation or whitepapers
Troubleshooting knowledge | Knowledge Center or AWS re:Post
Patterns and implementation guidance | AWS Prescriptive Guidance
Open an eligible support case | Support Center

aws-clf-technology-services#s3-class-dec.heading: S3 storage classes: access time, resilience and cost
excerpts: Choose an access model first, then compare retrieval delay, failure tolerance and total cost. Archive does not always mean delayed access: Glacier Instant Retrieval supports immediate reads, unlike restore-based archival classes.
S3 Standard | Frequent reads; multiple AZs.
S3 Standard-IA | Infrequent reads with immediate access and multi-AZ resilience; retrieval charges apply.
S3 One Zone-IA | Infrequent, recreatable objects; one AZ, so physical loss of that AZ can lose data.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering | Uncertain or changing access; automated tier selection, with eligible monitoring fees. Optional archive tiers introduce restore delays.
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval | Rare reads needing millisecond access; retrieval charges and minimum storage duration matter.
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval | Archive with a restore step; available retrieval options take minutes to hours.
S3 Glacier Deep Archive | Long-retained archives that tolerate hours of restore delay; Bulk retrieval can take up to 48 hours.

Durability is protection against data loss; availability is ability to access data when needed. A single-AZ class is a different risk choice from a multi-AZ class. Minimum storage-duration charges can apply even when an object is deleted sooner. Verify current regional pricing rather than memorizing a dollar rate.

Worked decision: A records team has seven-year retention, infrequent access, and a required four-hour response to a records request. Deep Archive is unsuitable if its restore time cannot meet that deadline. Compare an immediate-access class or a supported Flexible Retrieval option against both the deadline and retrieval cost. Retention length alone does not select a class; lifecycle movement must preserve the required access behavior.

Before changing a storage class, write down the maximum acceptable retrieval delay, whether data can be recreated, expected object size and retention, and the cost of requests, retrieval and transitions. A lifecycle rule manages eligible transitions or expiration; it does not prove a restore works.

Sources checked 2026-11-17: Amazon S3 User Guide, Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes; Understanding archive retrieval options. Textbook structure: Chapter 8, printed pages 139–142 (PDF pages 177–180). Current AWS documentation controls service behavior.

aws-clf-access-management#root-only-task.heading: Root-only tasks, credential storage and policy ownership
excerpts: Root-only tasks depend on account configuration. In a standalone account, the root user can restore permissions if its only IAM administrator locks itself out; closing the account also requires root credentials. With centralized root access enabled for an AWS Organizations member account, an authorized management account or delegated administrator can perform some privileged root tasks. That does not make every root task centrally available. Keep root protected and check the current task list for the exact account arrangement.
An application secret such as a database password | AWS Secrets Manager | Purpose-built secret lifecycle and rotation needs
A parameter or configuration value, optionally encrypted | AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store | Hierarchical parameter storage and application configuration
A reusable policy maintained by AWS | AWS managed policy | AWS owns updates; review its permissions before attaching
A reusable policy maintained by the customer | Customer-managed policy | Customer controls policy contents and updates; reusable across identities
A policy embedded in one identity | Inline policy | One-to-one attachment; not a reusable managed policy

Example: if an application needs a rotatable database credential, use Secrets Manager; if an operations team needs hierarchical configuration parameters, Parameter Store may fit. For permissions, select a customer-managed policy when your team must control a reusable permission set. An AWS-managed policy is convenient but its owner controls future changes.

aws-clf-security-compliance#credential-r.heading: Interpret an IAM credential report
excerpts: An IAM credential report is an account-level inventory of IAM users and selected IAM-managed credential status, including passwords, the first two access keys per user, MFA devices, and X.509 signing certificates. Use it to spot stale or unprotected IAM credentials during an audit. It does not show service-specific credentials or additional access keys beyond the first two; follow up with the relevant APIs or service tools when the question asks for complete visibility.

Example: a report shows an IAM user with an active access key and no MFA. That is evidence about the listed IAM credential, not proof that the user has no other credentials or that a workload uses no service-specific secret. Investigate the specific credential type and apply least privilege.

aws-clf-technology-services#file-gateway.heading: S3 File Gateway: local cache and cloud-backed objects
excerpts: Amazon S3 File Gateway presents file interfaces such as NFS or SMB while storing file data as objects in an S3 bucket. A local cache keeps recently accessed data available with lower latency; it is a performance cache, not the authoritative durable copy. Cache capacity affects how much recently used data can stay local. When a client accesses data that is not cached, the gateway retrieves it from S3. If applications write directly to the bucket outside the gateway, use cache refresh behavior so the gateway can discover changed objects.

Example: a branch office uses NFS for a shared dataset backed by S3 and repeatedly reads a small hot subset. File Gateway provides the familiar file protocol and local cache for that subset; S3 remains the cloud-backed store. Choose a different design if the requirement is block storage or a POSIX file system shared directly by cloud instances.

aws-clf-billing-support#commitment-shari.heading: Commitment scope, discount sharing and billing tags
excerpts: EC2 Reserved Instance flexibility is conditional on its attributes and scope. A regional RI can provide eligible instance-size flexibility for supported Linux/Unix shared-tenancy usage within the same family and Region; it does not reserve a particular Availability Zone’s capacity. A zonal RI is tied to an Availability Zone and can provide capacity reservation for matching usage, but does not provide regional size flexibility. Check current eligibility rules before treating an RI as interchangeable.

In AWS Organizations consolidated billing, eligible RI and Savings Plans discounts can be shared with linked accounts when discount sharing is enabled and the applicable ownership and billing settings permit it. The management account can control sharing preferences; a commitment is not a guaranteed discount for every account or workload. Review the payer and owner settings and actual eligible usage.

Billing tags have two sources: AWS-generated tags and user-defined tags. AWS or an AWS Marketplace seller creates and applies AWS-generated tags; customers define and apply user-defined tags. Both types must be activated separately for cost reporting. For historical correction, management-account users can request a backfill of the current activation status for up to 12 months, but cost data has tag values only for months when the resource tag was already present. A request cannot overlap another backfill and can be submitted only once every 24 hours; Cost Explorer, Data Exports, and the Cost and Usage Report refresh on their own cadence, so updated data is not immediate. A newly applied tag does not rewrite earlier resource history.

Example: a finance team wants to allocate next month’s EC2 costs by project. Apply a consistent user-defined Project tag, activate that cost allocation key, and allow time for it to appear in billing data. Separately check RI sharing configuration and eligible usage; neither tags nor consolidated billing alone guarantee that a particular account receives a commitment discount.

aws-clf-billing-support#partner-benefits.heading: Partner benefits and Marketplace purchase controls
excerpts: The AWS Partner Network serves organizations that build, sell, or deliver services around AWS. Depending on program, tier, eligibility, geography, and current terms, partner resources can include training and certification enablement, technical or go-to-market support, funding, and co-selling opportunities. Benefits are conditional; partner membership does not guarantee a particular discount, funding award, customer lead, or support entitlement.

AWS Marketplace is a catalog and procurement channel for third-party software, data, and services. Before purchase, an organization can govern who may discover, subscribe to, and deploy products through IAM permissions, procurement workflows, private offers, and organization-level controls. After purchase, an entitlement or license represents the rights granted for that product and contract; it is distinct from permission to administer AWS Marketplace itself. Eligible licenses can be shared across accounts using AWS License Manager, subject to product and subscription rules.

Example: a team needs a vendor security product for several AWS accounts. A buyer administrator reviews the offer and terms, restricts subscription rights to approved procurement roles, then uses the product’s supported license-sharing method. A Marketplace subscription is not an AWS Support plan, and an entitlement does not automatically grant every user permission to deploy the product.

q-aws-found-02.prompt: A workload must remain available if one data center location in a Region fails. Which design is the best starting point?
choices: Use one larger EC2 instance in the Region
Use a single subnet for the application
Use one edge location for the users
q-aws-found-02.explanation:
Use one larger EC2 instance in the Region — Incorrect. A larger instance in one place still stops when that location fails.
Use multiple Availability Zones — Correct. Placing the workload in more than one Availability Zone is the starting design when one location in the Region can fail.
Use a single subnet for the application — Incorrect. A single subnet stays in one Availability Zone, so it does not remove that location as a failure point.
Use one edge location for the users — Incorrect. An edge location shortens the path for distant users. It does not keep the regional workload up when one location fails.

Network ACL rules apply in whatever order a packet arrives
Security groups track connection state and network ACLs do not
q-aws-found-20.explanation:
Security groups and network ACLs both track connection state — Incorrect. Both controls do not track connection state. A security group does. A network ACL does not.

excerpts: Region vs Availability Zone
A Region is a geographic area; an Availability Zone is an isolated location inside a Region.
What is an edge location for?
Delivering supported edge/network services closer to users; it is not an Availability Zone.
Elasticity
Adjust capacity dynamically as demand changes.
Scalability
Increase or decrease capacity to support a larger or smaller workload.
CapEx vs OpEx
On-premises purchases are typically CapEx-heavy; cloud shifts more spending toward usage-based OpEx.
Well-Architected mindset
Evaluate architecture across security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, operational excellence, and sustainability.
Shared responsibility model
AWS secures the cloud infrastructure; customers secure data, identities, and many workload configurations.
IAM role
An assumable identity that provides temporary credentials and permissions.
Least privilege
Grant only permissions required for the task.
CloudTrail
Records account and API activity for auditing.
AWS Config
Tracks resource configuration history and evaluates configuration rules.
GuardDuty
Threat detection using AWS data sources.
Amazon EC2
Virtual machines when you need OS-level control.
AWS Lambda
Event-driven code without managing servers.
Auto Scaling vs load balancing
Auto Scaling changes capacity; load balancing distributes traffic.
Amazon S3
Object storage in buckets at massive scale.
Amazon EBS
Persistent block storage commonly attached to EC2 instances.
Amazon EFS
Managed shared file storage for Linux workloads.
Amazon VPC
A logically isolated network in AWS.
NAT gateway

Public NAT with an EIP, IGW and appropriate routes enables private-subnet IPv4 internet egress. Private NAT is for private connectivity, and native IPv6 outbound-only egress uses an egress-only IGW. Compare zonal and regional NAT availability designs.
Security group vs network ACL
Security groups are stateful resource-level controls; NACLs are stateless subnet-level controls.
Route 53
DNS, domain registration, health checks, and routing policies.
RDS Multi-AZ vs read replica
A single-standby RDS Multi-AZ DB instance provides failover with a non-readable standby. Multi-AZ DB clusters have readable standbys; asynchronous read replicas offload eligible reads and can lag.
DynamoDB
Managed key-value/document NoSQL database.
CloudWatch
Metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards.
Amazon SQS
Durable queue used to decouple asynchronous components.
Amazon SNS
Publish messages to multiple subscribers.
Amazon EventBridge
Routes events from sources to targets using rules.
AWS Pricing Calculator
Estimate the cost of a planned AWS architecture.
AWS Budgets vs Cost Explorer
Budgets tracks thresholds/alerts; Cost Explorer analyzes spend.
Cloud agility
Provision and change resources quickly instead of waiting on hardware procurement.
Economies of scale
Large providers spread infrastructure costs across many customers.
Rightsizing
Match resource size and type to actual workload requirements.
Hybrid cloud
Use cloud resources together with on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CAF
A framework to help organizations plan cloud adoption across business and technology perspectives.
High availability
Design so a service remains usable when components fail.
Fault tolerance
Continue operating through a failure with minimal interruption.
Migration driver
Common drivers include agility, elasticity, managed services, resilience, and reduced data-center ownership.
OpEx cloud model
Usage-based operating expense can replace some large up-front capital purchases.
Automation benefit
Repeatable automation reduces manual effort and configuration drift.
AWS Artifact
