Pricing Calculator purpose
Estimate costs before deploying a planned workload.
Cloud benefits under changing demand

Agility shortens the experiment/provisioning cycle; elasticity adjusts allocated capacity as demand changes. Scalability describes the ability to handle different load sizes, including planned growth. Managed services reduce undifferentiated work, but customers still design permissions, data protection, service configuration and recovery. Global infrastructure helps place workloads near users when data-governance requirements allow it.
Distinguish the six Well-Architected pillars

Operational excellence concerns operating, observing and improving workloads. Security concerns protecting information and systems; reliability concerns correct operation and recovery after disruption. A decision can affect several pillars: rightsizing can improve cost and sustainability, while redundant capacity may increase cost while improving reliability. Identify the primary business requirement rather than assuming every question is cost optimization.
Migration strategy, discovery and organizational readiness

CAF treats adoption as organizational transformation: business, people, governance, platform, security and operations perspectives require owners and an actionable readiness plan. Discover dependencies before migration. Application Migration Service supports server migration; DMS supports database movement/replication patterns; schema conversion may be needed for heterogeneous engines. A migration test includes data validation, cutover, rollback and business acceptance.
Economics, licensing and total cost

Compare total ownership: hardware refresh, facilities, power, cooling, staffing, resilience, software licenses and unused capacity. Usage-based cloud billing changes the cost model but does not guarantee savings. Rightsize from measured CPU, memory, I/O and business demand before making long commitments. Consider data transfer, idle storage, resilience and operational effort; economies of scale do not remove these line items.
Service-dependent responsibility boundaries

AWS operates physical facilities, hardware and foundational infrastructure. Customers choose access, data classification and application behavior. Shared controls such as patch management have different owners at different layers. Managed services do not transfer responsibility for granting least privilege or deciding whether regulated data may be stored in a chosen location. Verify the actual service model in the scenario.
Governance, encryption and audit evidence

Compliance evidence is contextual: Artifact supplies AWS reports/agreements, not an automatic certification of the customer workload. Verify the services, Regions, controls and regulatory requirements actually in use. At-rest encryption and TLS in transit protect different paths. KMS policies and IAM govern use of keys; encrypting a bucket does not by itself prevent an authorized principal from reading data.
Workforce access, root tasks and credentials

Prefer workforce federation through IAM Identity Center and an identity provider. IAM users are long-lived identities when required; groups organize user permissions, while roles are assumed to obtain temporary credentials. Separate authentication from authorization. Managed policies are reusable; inline policies attach to one identity. Least privilege requires actions, resources and conditions suited to the task. Store secrets appropriately rather than embedding them in code or images.
Preventive controls, findings and security resources

WAF filters supported application HTTP/S requests; Shield provides DDoS protection. Firewall Manager centrally manages supported security policies across accounts. GuardDuty detects threats; Inspector reports supported workload vulnerabilities; Macie discovers sensitive data in supported S3 content. Use official security documentation, Knowledge Center, the Security Blog and security/compliance resources to verify behavior. Marketplace offers third-party products; neither a listing nor a security-service subscription guarantees compliance.
Operate once, automate repeatedly

The console is useful for interactive exploration. CLI commands support scripts; SDKs integrate AWS APIs into application code. CloudFormation models infrastructure declaratively as templates/stacks, including dependencies and repeatable changes. Choose repeatability and change control for repeated environments. IaC still needs permissions, parameter validation, reviews and safe handling of state/data; a template is not proof that every deployment succeeded.
Availability scope and data residency

A Region contains multiple isolated AZs; an AZ contains one or more data centers. A subnet belongs to one AZ; a VPC is regional. Edge locations support selected edge/network services and are not replacement AZs. For residency, select permitted processing/storage locations; do not assume more Regions are always required or allowed. For global content delivery, distinguish edge caching from deploying a second application/database Region.
Compute families and scaling roles

General-purpose, compute-optimized, memory-optimized and storage-optimized instance families fit different bottlenecks. Measure CPU, memory, local I/O and networking rather than defaulting to the largest instance. Auto Scaling maintains/adjusts capacity; a load balancer distributes requests. Deployment across AZs and externalized session state are separate availability decisions.
Database models and migration responsibilities

RDS/Aurora fit relational workloads; DynamoDB provides key-value/document access patterns; ElastiCache supplies in-memory caching; Redshift is a data warehouse. These are workload models, not a ranking of universally better databases. DMS supports supported database migration/replication with cutover planning. Heterogeneous migrations can require schema conversion and application changes; moving rows does not prove all procedures, types and queries are compatible.
Network services and traffic paths

VPC routes select next hops; security groups and NACLs filter traffic at different scopes. Stateful security groups track return traffic; stateless NACL rules require the appropriate return path. Route 53 supplies DNS and routing policies. CloudFront supplies content delivery/caching; Global Accelerator improves paths to supported regional TCP/UDP endpoints. Match content distribution versus network acceleration requirements.
Storage classes, retrieval and recovery

S3 is object storage, EBS is persistent block storage in an AZ, instance store is ephemeral, and EFS/FSx provide file-system options. Select access model, sharing, persistence, latency and availability before price. Lifecycle can transition or expire eligible objects by date/age; versioning, replication and AWS Backup serve different recovery needs. A transition policy is not an immutable-retention control, and a replica is not proof of a tested restore.
AI/ML and analytics service selection

SageMaker AI supports building/training/deploying models; Lex builds conversational interfaces. A managed service does not eliminate data-quality, permissions, evaluation and governance decisions. Choose by the work: conversational intent, model training, ad hoc query, streaming processing, managed delivery, transformation or visualization. A multi-service pipeline may use several of these capabilities.
Recognize the service categories beyond core infrastructure

Integration: SQS queues work, SNS publishes to subscribers, EventBridge routes events, and Step Functions coordinates workflows. Select delivery and coordination behavior rather than matching the word event alone. Amplify supports frontend/mobile application development; IoT Core supports connecting/managing interactions with IoT devices. AWS Support is customer enablement. Verify current availability and the actual service capability before selecting a product merely by category.
Purchase commitments, capacity and transfer

On-Demand avoids a long-term commitment. Savings Plans commit an eligible hourly spend for a term; Reserved Instance discounts have scope/attribute rules. A regional RI discount does not itself reserve capacity in a selected AZ; capacity reservation is a separate requirement. Review RI flexibility and eligible consolidated-billing discount sharing within Organizations. Data transfer into/out of services, across AZs/Regions and to users has service-specific rules. Storage pricing includes requests, retrieval, minimum durations and transitions as well as stored GB.
Estimate, observe, allocate and alert

Pricing Calculator estimates a planned design from assumptions. Cost Explorer analyzes costs/usage and supports forecasts; detailed billing exports support more granular analysis. None of these validates a bad architecture assumption automatically. Organizations provides consolidated billing. Apply and activate eligible cost-allocation tag keys for billing analysis; merely attaching a tag does not guarantee its immediate appearance in reports. Account boundaries and allocation rules determine financial ownership.
Support choices and escalation resources

Current AWS documentation lists Basic Support and paid offerings including Business Support+, Enterprise Support and Unified Operations. Compare current technical-support scope, response targets and designated guidance rather than memorizing retired plan names or treating response targets as resolution guarantees. AWS Partners include software vendors and integrators; Marketplace distributes third-party products and purchasing entitlements. Professional Services and solutions architects address different assistance needs. Report suspected AWS-resource abuse through the appropriate Trust and Safety process, rather than sending it to an unrelated billing alert.
Customer reviews need sentiment, entities, and key phrases. Which service?
Amazon Comprehend; it analyzes meaning in text. Translate changes language; it is not the sentiment answer.
Text-to-speech vs speech-to-text
Amazon Polly converts text to spoken audio; Amazon Transcribe converts speech or recordings into text.
A support team needs the same article in several languages. Which service?
Amazon Translate; it translates text between supported languages. Comprehend analyzes text instead.
Build an application chatbot vs use an AWS AI assistant
Amazon Lex builds a conversational interface; Amazon Q is an AWS AI assistant. Choose by the product requirement.
Scanned form fields vs objects in a photograph
Amazon Textract extracts text and structured fields from documents; Amazon Rekognition analyzes images or video.
A team must build, train, and deploy its own ML model. Which service?
Amazon SageMaker AI. Do not choose it automatically when a prebuilt task-specific AI service already fits.
Run occasional SQL directly over files in S3
Amazon Athena; it provides serverless/ad hoc SQL queries over data in S3. It is not a warehouse.
Prepare and catalog data vs query data
AWS Glue integrates, transforms, and catalogs data; Amazon Athena queries data with SQL.
Process a large dataset with managed big-data frameworks
Amazon EMR; recognize the managed big-data processing use case without memorizing cluster administration.
Live telemetry stream vs durable application queue
Amazon Kinesis handles streaming data; Amazon SQS provides a durable asynchronous queue.
Search indexed logs/documents vs monitor metrics and alarms
Amazon OpenSearch Service searches and analyzes indexed data; Amazon CloudWatch monitors metrics, logs, and alarms.
Executives need business intelligence dashboards
Amazon Quick / Amazon Quick Sight capability for BI visualization. Athena is the ad hoc SQL query choice.
Analytics over a managed data warehouse
Amazon Redshift. RDS/Aurora serve relational application workloads; Redshift is the warehouse choice.
Query, transform, stream, search, visualize, or warehouse
Athena queries; Glue transforms/catalogs; Kinesis streams; OpenSearch searches; Quick/Quick Sight visualizes; Redshift warehouses.
Choose a prebuilt AI task service vs custom model workflow
Use the task-specific service when it fits: Comprehend, Lex, Polly, Transcribe, Translate, Rekognition, or Textract. Use SageMaker AI for a custom model workflow.
Employees already use a corporate identity provider for AWS access
Think IAM Identity Center and federation for centralized workforce access, not shared IAM-user credentials.
An EC2 application needs S3 access without stored keys
Use an IAM role with temporary credentials. Do not embed an IAM-user access key in the application.
Organize several IAM users versus provide an assumable identity
An IAM group organizes users; an IAM role is assumable and commonly supplies temporary credentials. A group is not a role.
Who are you versus what may you do?
Authentication proves identity with a password, MFA, federation, or session credentials. Authorization uses policies and permissions to decide allowed actions.
MFA versus a permissions policy
MFA adds an authentication factor; a permissions policy defines allowed or denied actions. MFA does not grant authorization.
Password complexity versus API permissions
An IAM account password policy controls IAM-user password requirements. A permissions policy controls actions and resources.
Routine administration with the AWS account root user
Protect root with strong MFA, avoid routine use and root access keys, and use named workforce identities. Some account tasks may still require root.
Access keys found in source code or an AMI
Treat them as exposed long-lived programmatic credentials: remove or rotate them and use roles with temporary credentials for workloads where supported.
Why prefer temporary credentials for a workload?
They reduce the exposure of long-lived access keys and are commonly delivered through an assumable IAM role.
Least privilege in an access scenario
Grant only the actions and resources required for the task; do not use root or broad credentials when a narrower role or policy fits.
Reusable policy versus one-identity policy
Managed policies are reusable; inline policies attach directly to one identity. Both are permission policies, not identities.
Application database password versus encryption key
Use AWS Secrets Manager for application secrets and AWS KMS for encryption key management. They are not interchangeable.
Temporary AWS permissions versus an application secret
An IAM role supplies temporary credentials and permissions to an assumable identity; Secrets Manager stores application secrets.
An applicable Allow and explicit Deny both exist
At recognition level, the explicit Deny wins. Policies provide authorization; authentication is a separate question.
Uncertain demand with no long-term commitment
On-Demand: flexible compute pricing without a long-term commitment; it is not automatically the cheapest option.
Interruption-tolerant batch workload
Spot uses spare capacity and can be interrupted. Include restart and business-impact tolerance.
Steady eligible compute usage with a commitment
Savings Plans provide pricing savings in exchange for an eligible compute-usage commitment; they do not by themselves reserve EC2 capacity.
Reserved Instance discount versus capacity guarantee
RI discount behavior depends on scope/attributes; Capacity Reservation separately reserves launch capacity.
Dedicated Host versus Dedicated Instance
Dedicated Host provides a dedicated physical server with host-level visibility/control. Dedicated Instance provides dedicated tenancy without that same host allocation model.
Storage cost beyond GB stored
Compare tier/class, requests, retrieval, minimum duration where applicable, lifecycle transitions, and transfer—not only stored volume.
Rarely accessed archive with long retrieval tolerance
Evaluate archival behavior, retrieval charges, and minimum duration rather than selecting only by the lowest storage rate.
Data-transfer cost decision
Inbound/outbound, inter-Region, inter-AZ, and service-to-service transfer have service-specific rules; placement affects cost.
RI behavior in AWS Organizations
Eligible RI discount sharing can depend on consolidated-billing organization settings; this is separate from reserving AZ capacity.
Guarantee launch capacity in a specific AZ
Capacity Reservation reserves capacity. A Savings Plan or RI primarily addresses discount behavior.
Estimate before deployment
Pricing Calculator models planned architecture cost from assumptions; it does not analyze actual spend.
Analyze actual spend and trends
Cost Explorer analyzes historical/current costs and usage and can support forecasts.
Alert when forecast spend crosses a threshold
Budgets provides configured alerts/actions; billing data and notifications can be delayed, so it is not a real-time hard cap.
Detailed cost and usage records
The Cost and Usage Report provides granular billing/usage data for reporting and analysis.
Attribute spend to a project or team
Use eligible cost allocation tags after activating the tag key for billing. Tagging does not erase charges or reconstruct history automatically.
Consolidate billing across accounts

Why a new billing tag or budget is not immediately visible
Billing data, tag activation, and notifications can have delay. These are reporting/alerting controls, not instantaneous charge prevention.
Calculator, Explorer, Budgets, and CUR
Calculator estimates; Explorer analyzes; Budgets alerts; CUR supplies detailed records.
Authoritative AWS technical reference
Use official AWS documentation and whitepapers for authoritative service behavior and reference information.
AWS troubleshooting knowledge articles
Knowledge Center provides support/troubleshooting knowledge; re:Post provides AWS-managed community Q&A.
Implementation patterns and strategies
Prescriptive Guidance provides patterns, strategies, and implementation guidance.
Open an eligible technical support case
Use Support Center; the available channel and response target depend on support entitlements.
Best-practice recommendations and checks
Trusted Advisor provides supported recommendations/checks. AWS Health reports health events instead.
Account or AWS service health event
AWS Health Dashboard/API provides operational health information; it is not the same as Trusted Advisor.
Suspected abuse of an AWS resource
Report it through Trust and Safety, not through Budgets or a technical recommendation tool.
Current AWS support-plan names

Recognize Basic Support, Business Support+, Enterprise Support, and Unified Operations. Basic is the general baseline; the enhanced tiers cue production, strategic business-critical, and mission-critical proactive operations needs respectively.
Legacy support names during the transition

Developer Support and Business Support stopped accepting new subscriptions on December 2, 2025 and are scheduled for discontinuation on January 1, 2027; Enterprise On-Ramp is also transitional. Do not present these as the current default paid-plan set.
Savings Plan versus Capacity Reservation
Savings Plans address eligible-compute pricing through commitment; Capacity Reservations address EC2 launch capacity in a specific Availability Zone. Discount is not capacity assurance.
Spot versus guaranteed capacity
Spot uses discounted spare capacity and can be interrupted. Choose it for interruption-tolerant work, not for a guaranteed launch-capacity requirement.
Invoice versus Cost Explorer
Bills/invoices represent charges owed; Cost Explorer analyzes current or historical cost and usage. Presentation can differ because refresh and data treatment are not identical.
Cost allocation tags versus consolidated billing
Cost allocation tags attribute spend to business dimensions after activation and availability; AWS Organizations supports account structure and consolidated billing.
Basic Support cue
Basic Support covers the general account/billing/documentation/community baseline. Do not imply it includes normal enhanced technical-support cases.
Business Support+ cue
Production workloads needing 24/7 technical support and AWS expert engagement cue Business Support+.
Enterprise Support cue
Business-critical workloads needing proactive strategic guidance and Technical Account Manager support cue Enterprise Support; it is more than faster response alone.
Unified Operations cue
Mission-critical workloads needing the highest proactive operations, resilience, and application-specific assistance cue Unified Operations. It is a support tier, not a generic managed service.
Discover or procure third-party software
AWS Marketplace provides third-party products/services and purchasing context; listings are not automatically AWS-native or compliant.
Transformation project and architecture guidance
Professional Services addresses AWS-delivered project expertise; solutions architects provide architecture guidance.
One component needs durable asynchronous work buffering
Amazon SQS: a queue decouples producers and consumers. SNS is fanout, not the durable queue cue.
One message must reach many subscribers
Amazon SNS: publish/subscribe fanout. SQS waits for consumers; EventBridge routes events by rules.
Events from sources need rule-based routing to targets
Amazon EventBridge: event routing. Step Functions coordinates workflow steps instead.
A process must coordinate several workflow steps
AWS Step Functions: workflow orchestration. EventBridge routes events but does not represent the multi-step workflow cue.
Cloud contact-center requirement
Amazon Connect: cloud contact center. Amazon SES is the application-email choice.
An application needs transactional or bulk email
Amazon SES: application email. SNS is notification fanout, not the dedicated email-service cue.
Compile, build, and test source code
AWS CodeBuild: build. CodePipeline orchestrates delivery stages after or around the build.
Orchestrate software delivery stages
AWS CodePipeline: pipeline. CodeBuild performs the build step; it is not the delivery orchestrator.
Trace one request across distributed services
AWS X-Ray: distributed tracing. CloudWatch provides monitoring signals, not this specific trace cue.
Users need one remotely streamed application, not a full desktop
Amazon AppStream 2.0: application streaming. WorkSpaces provides a managed desktop.
Users need a managed virtual desktop environment
Amazon WorkSpaces: desktop. AppStream streams applications; Secure Browser is browser-only access.
Users need secure browser-based access without a full desktop
Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser: browser. It is distinct from WorkSpaces desktop and AppStream application streaming.
Develop and deploy a frontend web or mobile application
AWS Amplify: frontend/mobile application platform at recognition level. It is not CodeBuild's generic build role.
Connect and manage interactions with IoT devices
AWS IoT Core: device connectivity and device-to-cloud interaction at recognition level.
The requirement is AWS business or technical assistance
AWS Support: customer enablement. Use the Domain 4 material for support-plan and entitlement details.
Queue, fanout, route, coordinate, build, pipeline, trace, app, desktop, browser, frontend, device
SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Step Functions, CodeBuild, CodePipeline, X-Ray, AppStream, WorkSpaces, Secure Browser, Amplify, IoT Core. Match the business verb first.
Why might an organization migrate to AWS?

Possible outcomes include reduced business risk, improved ESG performance, increased revenue opportunity, greater agility, and improved operational efficiency. Choose the stated business outcome rather than assuming migration always means lower cost.
Technical skills exist, but ownership, governance, and the operating model are missing
This is an AWS Cloud Adoption Framework readiness concern. CAF organizes business and technology adoption concerns; it is not solved merely by selecting EC2.
Leave the data center quickly with minimal application changes
Rehost: move with minimal code change. It may be a first step before later modernization.
Move while adopting selected managed-service improvements
Replatform: make limited optimizations without fully redesigning the application.
Modernization is the goal and substantial redesign is acceptable
Refactor or re-architect: change the application substantially to use cloud-native capabilities.
Replace the existing application with a different product or SaaS model
Repurchase: change the software/product model instead of migrating the old implementation.
Workload is either unnecessary or must stay where it is for now
Retire removes an unneeded workload; retain defers migration. Do not migrate an application that should be retired.
Before moving 100 servers, the team needs utilization and dependency information
Perform discovery and assessment first. Identify applications, servers, dependencies, utilization, data, network relationships, and business criticality.
Move or replicate a database during a migration
AWS Database Migration Service can support database movement/replication patterns. DMS does not select the business strategy or prove application compatibility.
General server or application migration
AWS Application Migration Service is the recognition-level migration resource. It is not a readiness assessment or a replacement for validation.
Transfer online data between storage locations
AWS DataSync supports online data transfer. Data transfer alone does not migrate application behavior or dependencies.
What does database replication help with, and what does it not prove?
Replication can synchronize source and target before cutover and reduce downtime. It does not prove schema, data type, query, transaction, or application compatibility.
What must happen before declaring a migration successful?
Validate dependencies, application behavior, data integrity, security controls, business acceptance, and cutover checks; define rollback if a required check fails.
Migration traps to separate
Rehost is not refactor; DMS is not a strategy; replication is not compatibility validation; discovery precedes migration; CAF includes organizational readiness.
Which pillar handles failure recovery?
Reliability: design to continue and recover when components fail.
Reliability versus Performance Efficiency
Reliability is resilience and recovery; Performance Efficiency is effective resource and technology use.
Cost Optimization versus Sustainability
Cost Optimization targets unnecessary spend; Sustainability targets environmental impact.

Reduce environmental impacts of cloud workloads.

Physical infrastructure owner

Compliance reports
AWS Artifact provides AWS compliance reports and agreements, not live monitoring.
CloudWatch cue

CloudTrail cue

AWS Config cue

Encryption at rest versus in transit

Customer compliance

AWS WAF
Filter web requests with web ACL rules; it is not the general DDoS answer.

DDoS protection.

Human, graphical, one-time inspection
AWS Management Console: interactive browser-based administration.
Repeatable shell administration
AWS CLI: command-line access that can be scripted and reviewed.
Application code needs AWS
AWS SDK: programmatic service access from application code.
Programmatic service access concept
AWS services expose APIs; CLF recognition does not require request signing or HTTP implementation.
Repeatable, versioned infrastructure
Infrastructure as code, such as CloudFormation, defines desired resources in a reviewable form.
Cloud, hybrid, or on-premises?
Cloud runs in cloud infrastructure; on-premises remains customer-controlled; hybrid combines both. Hybrid is not synonymous with multi-cloud.
One-time task versus recurring process
One-off human inspection favors Console; recurring consistent provisioning favors CLI automation or IaC.
Geographic AWS area
A Region contains multiple Availability Zones and is a primary choice for geography and residency.
Independent failure domain within a Region
An Availability Zone is an isolated location within a Region; multiple AZs support high availability.
Closer to geographically dispersed users
Edge locations support selected edge services and can reduce delivery latency; they are not AZs.
Survive one AZ failure
Multi-AZ improves availability within a Region.
Regional disaster, locality, or sovereignty decision
Multi-Region can address regional recovery or approved geographic needs, but is not required for every workload.
Data must remain in a permitted geography
Choose permitted Regions first; do not treat global replication or edge delivery as automatically acceptable.
VM control and long-running custom software
Amazon EC2 provides virtual machines with substantial guest-OS control.
Event-driven function without server management
AWS Lambda runs suitable functions while AWS manages the underlying servers.
Compute, memory, or storage bottleneck
Compute optimized targets CPU; memory optimized targets memory; storage optimized targets local storage throughput; general purpose balances resources.
Container orchestration choice

Containers without managing servers
Fargate is serverless compute for supported container workloads; ECS/EKS remain orchestration choices.
Capacity versus traffic
Auto Scaling adjusts the amount of compute; a load balancer distributes traffic across targets.
Explicit Kubernetes requirement
Choose EKS. Do not infer Kubernetes from the generic word containers.
Fargate versus Lambda
Fargate runs containers; Lambda runs functions. Serverless describes management responsibility, not one universal runtime.
High-yield Domain 3 traps
CLI ≠ SDK; Region ≠ AZ; AZ ≠ edge; Multi-AZ ≠ Multi-Region; ECS ≠ EKS; Fargate ≠ orchestrator; Auto Scaling ≠ load balancing.
Managed versus EC2-hosted database
EC2-hosted gives more OS/software control and responsibility; managed services reduce selected infrastructure burden but do not remove customer data and access duties.
Relational SQL workload
Amazon RDS is the managed relational database cue.
Managed MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible relational option
Amazon Aurora is an AWS-managed relational database option.
Key-value or document access
Amazon DynamoDB is the managed NoSQL key-value/document database cue.
Repeated reads need low latency
Amazon ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caching; it is not automatically the durable system of record.
Move or replicate database data
AWS Database Migration Service supports data movement and replication patterns.
Change database engines
AWS Schema Conversion Tool helps assess and convert schema or database code; it is not a general data-transfer tool.
DMS versus SCT
DMS moves/replicates data; SCT helps convert schema/code. Neither alone proves application compatibility.
Logically isolated AWS network
Amazon VPC is the isolated virtual network; a subnet is a segment inside it.
Network segment inside a VPC
A subnet separates placement; public/private behavior depends on routing and associated configuration.
Stateful resource-level traffic control
Security groups allow traffic at the resource or network-interface level and are stateful.
Stateless subnet-level traffic control
Network ACLs filter at the subnet boundary and are stateless.
Supported workload vulnerability and exposure assessment
Amazon Inspector identifies supported vulnerabilities and unintended exposure; it is not a firewall.
Domain-name routing
Amazon Route 53 provides DNS and domain-name routing; it is not a load balancer or VPN.
Encrypted connection over the internet
AWS VPN provides encrypted network connectivity over an internet path.
Dedicated private network path
AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity; it does not automatically encrypt traffic.
Network confusion pairs
VPC ≠ subnet; security group is stateful/resource-level; NACL is stateless/subnet-level; Inspector ≠ firewall; VPN ≠ Direct Connect.
Object storage
Amazon S3 stores objects such as files, static assets, backups and data-lake content.
S3 access-pattern choice
Frequent, infrequent, archive and changing/unknown access patterns lead to different S3 storage-class reasoning.
Age-based object management
S3 Lifecycle transitions or expires eligible objects by rules; it is not a universal backup strategy.
Persistent EC2 block device
Amazon EBS provides persistent block storage for EC2.
Temporary local block storage
Instance store is fast local storage tied to instance/host lifecycle and is ephemeral.
Shared Linux file storage
Amazon EFS provides managed shared file-system semantics for Linux-oriented workloads.
Specific managed file-system technology
Amazon FSx provides managed file systems for specific technologies and use cases.
Hybrid storage integration
AWS Storage Gateway connects on-premises environments with AWS-backed storage patterns.
Centralized backup policies
AWS Backup manages backups for supported AWS resources; backup is distinct from replication and lifecycle.
Object, block, file
S3 = object; EBS = block; EFS/FSx = file. Choose by access model, not by a generic storage label.
Storage confusion pairs
S3 ≠ EBS; EBS ≠ instance store; EFS ≠ S3; lifecycle ≠ backup; replication ≠ tested restore.
Elasticity versus scalability
Scalability handles a larger workload; elasticity dynamically adjusts capacity as demand changes. Planned growth cues scalability; temporary unpredictable spikes cue elasticity.
Agility versus elasticity
Agility is faster provisioning, deployment and experimentation than traditional procurement. Elasticity is capacity changing with demand; agility is not simply scaling up and down.
Availability, resilience and fault tolerance
Availability means access when needed; resilience means withstanding or recovering from disruption; fault tolerance aims to continue operating through a failure. Architecture is still required.
Global reach is not automatic redundancy
Regions and global infrastructure provide geographic choices for user proximity, sovereignty and resilience. They do not automatically create low latency, compliance or multi-Region failover.
Economies of scale
AWS can spread infrastructure investment and purchasing power across customers. This can help economics but never guarantees every workload costs less.
Variable expense and upfront commitment
Usage-based cloud consumption can reduce premature peak-capacity purchases and shift portions of spending toward variable use. It does not eliminate every upfront or operating cost.
Managed services and shared responsibility
Managed services reduce selected infrastructure maintenance work. Customers still handle data, permissions, configuration and other responsibilities under the service boundary.
Cloud benefit versus guaranteed outcome
Cloud benefits enable choices; they do not guarantee lower cost, compliance, availability or low latency without an appropriate architecture and operation.
Total Cost of Ownership
TCO includes hardware, facilities, power, cooling, networking, maintenance, staffing, licensing, refresh/replacement and operational labor—not only purchase price or a monthly cloud bill.
Fixed versus variable cost
Traditional capacity purchases often commit money before demand is known. Usage-based consumption can vary with use, but cloud is not automatically cheaper and may still have commitments.
Rightsizing versus autoscaling
Rightsizing selects appropriate resource capacity from measured requirements. Autoscaling adjusts quantity or capacity over time as demand changes; they solve different problems.
Utilization versus availability
Utilization is how much capacity is used; availability is access when needed. Redundant capacity can improve availability without being fully utilized.
Cost optimization
Optimize by rightsizing, removing idle resources, selecting appropriate services, automating operations and matching capacity to requirements—not by choosing the cheapest direct price alone.
Managed-service economics
Compare service price with maintenance, staffing, reliability, licensing and time-to-market. A managed service may reduce operational labor without having the lowest direct resource price.
Licensing and cloud economics
Check license portability, license-included terms and host or tenancy requirements. A Dedicated Host may address a physical-host constraint but is not automatically cheapest.
Cloud is not automatically cheaper
Compare demand, utilization, storage, transfer, resilience, licensing, operations and staffing. Economies of scale can help but do not replace workload-specific analysis.
Idle capacity
Peak provisioning, future-growth buffers and forgotten resources can create waste. Measure demand, then stop, remove, resize or schedule resources when requirements allow.
Rarely accessed archive objects must open immediately.
Evaluate S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval; Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive require a restore. Include retrieval and minimum-duration costs.
When is S3 One Zone-IA a reasonable risk tradeoff?
For infrequently accessed objects that can be recreated or recovered elsewhere, when single-AZ loss is acceptable. It is not equivalent to multi-AZ resilience.
Does deleting an archive early end all storage charges?
Not necessarily. Minimum storage-duration charges can apply; include retrieval, request and transition costs in the comparison.

q-clf-gap-root-01.prompt: An organization manages an AWS member account with centralized root access enabled. Its account operator must perform a privileged root task but should not create or use the member account root password. What is the best first step?
choices: Disable Organizations and use root for routine administration
Use the management account for eligible root tasks
Attach AdministratorAccess and treat it as root
Create a shared IAM user called root
q-clf-gap-root-01.explanation: Disable Organizations and use root for routine administration: This is not the recommended workflow and root should not be used for routine administration. Use the management account for eligible root tasks: Correct for some tasks when centralized root is enabled and the task supports delegated privileged access; verify the exact operation. Attach AdministratorAccess and treat it as root: AdministratorAccess is an IAM permission policy and is not equivalent to root credentials or all root-only operations. Create a shared IAM user called root: An IAM user with that name remains an IAM principal and is not the AWS account root user.
q-clf-gap-root-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-credential-report-01.prompt: An auditor downloads an IAM credential report and sees only two access-key rows for a user. What conclusion is valid?
choices: Every credential category is shown, including more than two keys
All service-specific keys used by workloads appear in this report
API access permissions can be read directly from the credential list
The report omits extra access keys and service-specific credentials
q-clf-gap-credential-report-01.explanation: Every credential category is shown, including more than two keys: The report covers selected IAM-managed credentials, not every credential category. All service-specific keys used by workloads appear in this report: Service-specific credentials are explicitly outside the report scope. API access permissions can be read directly from the credential list: Credential status does not list the user’s effective API permissions. The report omits extra access keys and service-specific credentials: Correct: the report includes only the first two IAM access keys and excludes additional keys and service-specific credentials.
q-clf-gap-credential-report-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-gateway-cache-01.prompt: A branch office accesses files through Amazon S3 File Gateway. Which statement describes the local cache correctly?
choices: It retains recently accessed data for lower-latency access while the S3 bucket stores the cloud-backed objects
It is the only durable copy of every file, while S3 is only a metadata index
It converts the gateway into an EBS block volume for EC2
It guarantees that changes made directly in S3 appear immediately without cache refresh behavior
q-clf-gap-gateway-cache-01.explanation: It retains recently accessed data for lower-latency access while the S3 bucket stores the cloud-backed objects: File Gateway retains recently accessed data locally for performance while using S3 for cloud-backed object data. It is the only durable copy of every file, while S3 is only a metadata index: the cache is not the only durable copy; the S3 bucket stores the file data as objects. It converts the gateway into an EBS block volume for EC2: File Gateway is a file interface, not an EBS block volume. It guarantees that changes made directly in S3 appear immediately without cache refresh behavior: direct S3 changes can require cache refresh behavior before the gateway’s cached view reflects them.
q-clf-gap-gateway-cache-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-ri-flex-01.prompt: A team wants an EC2 Reserved Instance discount to apply across matching instance sizes in one Region and does not need guaranteed capacity in a particular Availability Zone. Which scope is the closest fit?
choices: A regional Reserved Instance, subject to supported platform, tenancy, and family flexibility rules
A zonal Reserved Instance because it has the broadest size flexibility
An On-Demand Capacity Reservation because it creates a discount across Regions
A Spot Instance because it guarantees uninterrupted capacity
q-clf-gap-ri-flex-01.explanation: A regional Reserved Instance, subject to supported platform, tenancy, and family flexibility rules: a regional RI can provide eligible size flexibility within a family and Region, subject to attributes such as platform and tenancy; it does not reserve one AZ. A zonal Reserved Instance because it has the broadest size flexibility: zonal RIs are scoped to an AZ and are associated with matching capacity reservation, not the broadest regional size flexibility. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation because it creates a discount across Regions: an On-Demand Capacity Reservation reserves matching capacity but does not create a cross-Region RI discount. A Spot Instance because it guarantees uninterrupted capacity: Spot capacity can be interrupted and is not a guarantee of uninterrupted capacity.
q-clf-gap-ri-flex-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-ri-share-01.prompt: A linked account has eligible EC2 usage, but a Reserved Instance discount owned by another organization account is not being applied. What should the billing administrator check first?
choices: Whether discount sharing is enabled for the relevant owner and linked accounts and whether the usage is eligible
Whether the linked account has activated a cost allocation tag
Whether the RI is an IAM managed policy
Whether the EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address
q-clf-gap-ri-share-01.explanation: Whether discount sharing is enabled for the relevant owner and linked accounts and whether the usage is eligible: the organization’s sharing settings, owner/account activation, and usage eligibility determine whether the discount can be applied. Whether the linked account has activated a cost allocation tag: cost allocation tags help analyze cost and do not enable RI sharing. Whether the RI is an IAM managed policy: IAM managed policies control permissions and are unrelated to RI ownership or billing preferences. Whether the EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address: a public IPv4 address does not affect RI discount sharing eligibility.
q-clf-gap-ri-share-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-tags-01.prompt: A finance analyst applied a user-defined Project tag today and needs it in billing reports. What additional step is required?
choices: Activate the user-defined cost allocation tag key in Billing and Cost Management and allow processing time
Change the tag to an AWS-generated key with the same name
Add the tag only to the payer account
Assume activation will rewrite usage from before the tag was applied
q-clf-gap-tags-01.explanation: Activate the user-defined cost allocation tag key in Billing and Cost Management and allow processing time: Correct: both AWS-generated and user-defined cost allocation tag keys must be activated separately and processing can take up to 24 hours. Change the tag to an AWS-generated key with the same name: Incorrect: customer-defined tags remain user-defined; renaming does not make AWS the tag creator. Add the tag only to the payer account: Incorrect: the tag must be applied to the resource whose usage is being attributed; tagging only a payer account does not label member resources. Assume activation will rewrite usage from before the tag was applied: Incorrect: AWS permits eligible management-account users to backfill activation status for up to 12 months when the tag historically existed on the resource, but it cannot populate months before the tag was present.
q-clf-gap-tags-01.review: New original scenario; every option is addressed in the explanation.

q-clf-gap-partner-benefits-01.explanation: No specific funding, discount, lead, or support entitlement is guaranteed; available benefits depend on program eligibility and current terms: Correct: the exam guide names partner training/certification, events and volume discounts, but actual programs and eligibility determine which benefits apply; no specific benefit is guaranteed by membership alone. Every partner receives a fixed AWS service discount: Incorrect: AWS describes eligible training discounts or credits, not a universal service discount for every partner. Assume a Marketplace entitlement automatically grants deployment permission to every user
q-clf-gap-marketplace-governance-01.explanation: Restrict buyer subscription permissions through IAM/procurement governance, then use the product-supported License Manager sharing workflow when eligible: govern subscription rights with buyer permissions and procurement controls; share eligible licenses through the product-supported License Manager workflow. Give every employee Marketplace administrator permissions and assume entitlements restrict subscriptions: broad administrator access weakens governance, and an entitlement does not independently restrict who can subscribe. Use AWS Support Center to issue Marketplace licenses: Support Center handles support cases, not third-party software licensing. q-clf-gap-transfer-costs-01.prompt: A team uploads data to a service, transfers some data to another Region, and later serves data to internet users. Which pricing review is most accurate?
choices: Treat inbound transfer as generally uncharged, then check the service-specific outbound and inter-Region rules and any request charges
Assume every byte entering AWS is charged and all outbound transfer is free
Assume all same-Region and cross-Region transfers are free if both endpoints use AWS
Compare only stored gigabytes because transfer and request charges are included in storage
q-clf-gap-transfer-costs-01.explanation: Treat inbound transfer as generally uncharged, then check the service-specific outbound and inter-Region rules and any request charges: Correct. AWS states that most inbound transfer and same-Region service-to-service transfer is not charged, while outbound/inter-Region paths and service rules can differ; requests can still be billable. Assume every byte entering AWS is charged and all outbound transfer is free: Incorrect. This reverses the general inbound/outbound pattern and ignores service-specific rules. Assume all same-Region and cross-Region transfers are free if both endpoints use AWS: Incorrect. Same-Region and cross-Region behavior is not interchangeable, and exceptions apply. Compare only stored gigabytes because transfer and request charges are included in storage: Incorrect. Storage, requests, retrieval, and data transfer can be separate cost dimensions.

q-clf-gap-bill-source-01.prompt: A finance analyst needs the final amount owed for a closed AWS billing period. Cost Explorer shows a different analytical total. Which source should establish the amount owed?
choices: The issued AWS invoice; use Cost Explorer to analyze trends and investigate the presentation difference
A Cost Explorer forecast, because forecasts supersede closed-period billing
The Pricing Calculator, because it estimates the deployed architecture
A cost allocation tag report, because tags determine the invoice total
q-clf-gap-bill-source-01.explanation: The issued AWS invoice; use Cost Explorer to analyze trends and investigate the presentation difference: Correct. AWS describes the invoice as the final amount owed; analytical data can differ in timing, grouping, granularity, rounding, and treatment of discounts, credits, refunds, or taxes. A Cost Explorer forecast, because forecasts supersede closed-period billing: Incorrect. A forecast estimates a period and is not the payable invoice. The Pricing Calculator, because it estimates the deployed architecture: Incorrect. The calculator estimates planned use from assumptions; it does not determine charges already invoiced. A cost allocation tag report, because tags determine the invoice total: Incorrect. Cost allocation tags organize cost views; they do not replace the invoice as the amount owed.
q-clf-gap-bill-source-01.review: New focused scenario reviewed against current AWS documentation on 2026-11-18; every option explained.

q-clf-assess-41-mixed-purchase-01.prompt: A service has a predictable EC2 baseline that may justify a usage commitment, a restartable nightly queue, and a release tier that must be launchable in one chosen Availability Zone. Which plan separates the three constraints?
choices: Evaluate a Savings Plan for eligible baseline use, Spot for restartable queue work, and an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the selected-AZ launch requirement
Use On-Demand for the predictable baseline, Spot for queue and release capacity, and rely on instance selection to hold launch capacity in the chosen AZ
Use a regional RI for the predictable baseline, Spot for the restartable queue, and assume regional size flexibility reserves launch capacity in the release AZ
Use Savings Plans for baseline and queue, then rely on the compute-usage commitment to reserve launch capacity in the selected AZ when the release arrives
q-clf-assess-41-mixed-purchase-01.explanation: Evaluate a Savings Plan for eligible baseline use, Spot for restartable queue work, and an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the selected-AZ launch requirement: Correct. A usage commitment can discount eligible baseline usage, Spot can fit interruptible queue work, and a separate Capacity Reservation addresses the selected-AZ capacity requirement. Use On-Demand for the predictable baseline, Spot for queue and release capacity, and rely on instance selection to hold launch capacity in the chosen AZ: Incorrect. Spot can be interrupted, and changing a bid does not turn Spot into guaranteed capacity. Use a regional RI for the predictable baseline, Spot for the restartable queue, and assume regional size flexibility reserves launch capacity in the release AZ: Incorrect. A regional RI discount does not reserve capacity in a chosen AZ, and an RI does not make an interruptible queue interruption-proof. Use Savings Plans for baseline and queue, then rely on the compute-usage commitment to reserve launch capacity in the selected AZ when the release arrives: Incorrect. Savings Plans are pricing commitments for eligible usage, not capacity reservations; they do not make Spot usage uninterrupted.
q-clf-assess-41-mixed-purchase-01.review: Original integrated decision scenario checked against current official AWS sources on 2026-11-18; every option explained.

q-clf-assess-42-budget-action-01.prompt: A finance team receives a budget alert after charges have accrued and asks AWS Budgets to stop every service exactly when spend reaches its threshold. Which response is most accurate?
choices: Treat the alert as monitoring; configure only supported budget actions with the required permissions, and do not treat them as a universal instantaneous spending cap
Increase the evaluation frequency, confirm notification delivery, and rely on Budgets to stop every AWS service at the threshold before another charge accrues
Switch to a forecasted budget and choose an account-wide action, assuming the forecast automatically blocks launches across all services at its threshold
Activate every cost-allocation tag, attach the budget to those tags, and expect AWS to throttle tagged resources automatically when the limit is reached
q-clf-assess-42-budget-action-01.explanation: Treat the alert as monitoring; configure only supported budget actions with the required permissions, and do not treat them as a universal instantaneous spending cap: Correct. AWS documents supported budget actions and required permissions; billing data and notifications can be delayed, and the actions are not a universal hard cap across every service. Increase the evaluation frequency, confirm notification delivery, and rely on Budgets to stop every AWS service at the threshold before another charge accrues: Incorrect. More frequent evaluation does not create an all-service stop guarantee or remove data delay. Switch to a forecasted budget and choose an account-wide action, assuming the forecast automatically blocks launches across all services at its threshold: Incorrect. A forecast is a monitoring signal, not an enforcement policy. Activate every cost-allocation tag, attach the budget to those tags, and expect AWS to throttle tagged resources automatically when the limit is reached: Incorrect. Tags organize eligible cost data after activation; they neither stop resource usage nor enforce a budget.
q-clf-assess-42-budget-action-01.review: Original integrated decision scenario checked against current official AWS sources on 2026-11-18; every option explained.

q-clf-assess-43-health-case-01.prompt: An EC2 event appears in AWS Health with affected resource IDs. The application team needs both to confirm the AWS event's scope and to request technical troubleshooting. Which sequence matches the two needs?
choices: Review the event and affected resources in AWS Health, then open a technical case in Support Center if the account's plan permits it
Use Trusted Advisor to verify the account-specific outage and affected EC2 resources, then use Cost Explorer to create a technical support case for the service team
Open Support Center alone to retrieve the Health event and affected resource list; technical case access is available even on Basic Support
Subscribe to Marketplace diagnostics, then post the event details and resource IDs on re:Post to create a private technical support case
q-clf-assess-43-health-case-01.explanation: Review the event and affected resources in AWS Health, then open a technical case in Support Center if the account's plan permits it: Correct. AWS Health presents event details and affected-resource information; Support Center is the case-management path when the account has the required technical-support entitlement. Use Trusted Advisor to verify the account-specific outage and affected EC2 resources, then use Cost Explorer to create a technical support case for the service team: Incorrect. Trusted Advisor provides supported recommendations/checks, while Cost Explorer analyzes costs; neither performs both stated tasks. Open Support Center alone to retrieve the Health event and affected resource list; technical case access is available even on Basic Support: Incorrect. Health is the event and affected-resource source, and technical cases depend on the account's support entitlement. Subscribe to Marketplace diagnostics, then post the event details and resource IDs on re:Post to create a private technical support case: Incorrect. Marketplace is for third-party products and re:Post is a community resource, not the private Support Center case channel.
q-clf-assess-43-health-case-01.review: Original integrated decision scenario checked against current official AWS sources on 2026-11-18; every option explained.
